name: Tripeptide-29
lead: Tripeptide-29 is a short peptide made of three amino acids, glycine, proline and hydroxyproline (Gly-Pro-Hyp), which is the repeating unit of collagen. It is used in firming and anti-aging skincare, added to creams, serums and neck products, with the aim of making skin look firmer, smoother and more resilient. Collagen loss and fragmentation are central to how aging skin sags and wrinkles, which is why collagen-fragment ingredients are marketed for appearance.

It belongs to the family of cosmetic peptides sometimes called matrikines or signal peptides, which are fragments of structural proteins that suppliers say prompt skin cells to make new collagen. Another cosmetic peptide in this family, palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (Matrixyl), launched in 2000 [2]. In the United States such products are regulated as cosmetics, and the FDA says US law does not recognise cosmeceuticals as a category [1].

Published human trials on topical tripeptide-29 itself are not available. Collagen peptides taken by mouth have been studied in randomised trials for skin hydration, elasticity and wrinkling [3][4][5], and a 2026 review of aesthetic-dermatology peptides concluded that peptide products should be judged individually rather than treated as interchangeable [6].

chain: A collagen-fragment peptide is applied to the skin daily
It is proposed to signal fibroblasts to build collagen

angle.text: Tripeptide-29 is applied in a cream or serum to improve the look of skin firmness and fine lines. The firming mechanism comes from supplier descriptions of collagen signalling, while human data come from related oral collagen peptide trials [3][4][5].

paras: Tripeptide-29 is found in firming serums, neck creams and anti-aging moisturizers, sometimes alongside other peptides. Users apply it daily in the hope of firmer-looking skin and softer fine lines.

Marketing for collagen creams has drawn celebrity coverage; for example, entertainment press has reported on a well-known actress describing a collagen cream from a mainstream skincare brand as part of her routine.[9] Collagen products also appear in supplement form, where news and lifestyle outlets compare whole collagen with hydrolysed collagen peptides.[10]

Gly-Pro-Hyp is the repeating triplet of the collagen triple helix, which is why it is used as the building block of collagen-mimetic peptides in laboratory work.[7] Skincare suppliers list the ingredient under the name tripeptide-29 and present it as a collagen fragment that is small enough to be formulated into creams and serums.

Cosmetic peptides are often grouped as matrikines, a term for messenger peptides that interact with specific cell receptors and are described as switching on genes involved in renewing the extracellular matrix.[2] The best-known example, palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, was launched by the French ingredient maker Sederma in 2000 under the trade name Matrixyl; it carries a 16-carbon fatty chain that is said to help it penetrate the skin's lipid layers, and the company and independent groups have published laboratory and in vivo studies on it.[2]

Matrikine-type peptides are fragments of structural proteins. Suppliers say such fragments signal skin cells that collagen is being broken down and prompt new collagen synthesis. Matrixyl, launched in 2000, is classed in the same family [2].
Collagen-mimetic peptides, whose repeating unit is the Gly-Pro-Hyp motif, have been used since the late 1960s as tools to study collagen and to develop collagen-based biomaterials [7].

Cosmetics in the US do not require pre-market approval of claims, and the FDA states that the law does not recognise cosmeceuticals as a category [1]. Mild irritation is possible on sensitive skin, as with most cosmetic actives.

sections.h: Collagen and the look of skin
paras: Collagen is the main structural protein of the dermis and gives skin tensile strength and support. Its chains form a triple helix in which glycine recurs at roughly every third position and the sequence is typically Gly-Pro-X or Gly-X-Hyp, with hydroxyproline (Hyp) stabilising the helix through extra hydrogen bonds.[13] Gly-Pro-Hyp is therefore the most characteristic repeat of the molecule, which is the reason the tripeptide is often described as a collagen fragment.[7]

With age the dermis thins, the collagen network is reduced and altered, and the elastic fibre network degrades, while long-term sun exposure further disorganises collagen and elastic fibres; these changes are linked to the sagging, roughness and lines associated with aging and photoaging.[13] Skincare ingredients built around collagen fragments are aimed at this part of appearance: the visible firmness and smoothness of the skin surface and the neck.

Products containing tripeptide-29 are typically leave-on formulas, such as serums, eye and neck creams and night moisturisers, applied once or twice a day. They are often layered with other peptides, hyaluronic acid or retinoids in a general anti-aging routine, and users commonly describe wanting firmer-looking skin around the jawline, neck and cheeks as a goal. Results in marketing language are usually described as appearing over several weeks of regular use, which matches the timescale used in oral collagen trials (four to twelve weeks).[3]

Whole collagen is a large protein, and the encyclopedic literature notes that intact collagen in creams is too large to enter the skin; for this reason cosmetics more often use hydrolysed collagen or small peptides such as glycyl-prolyl-hydroxyproline, on the premise that smaller fragments are absorbed more readily.[13] That absorption premise is described there as unproven, and the same source states that, as of 2025, clinical evidence that oral or topical collagen improves wrinkles or skin aging is lacking, in contrast to the positive findings reported in the individual supplement trials below.[13]

On the oral side, hydrolysed collagen is digested into peptides and amino acids; the trial authors who report skin benefits propose that circulating peptides such as Gly-Pro-Hyp reach fibroblasts and stimulate matrix production, whereas critics note that the ingested protein is broken down like any dietary protein.[3][13] Both views appear in the literature, and trials are mostly funded by supplement manufacturers, a point researchers in the field raise when discussing the body of work.

No studies found on topical tripeptide-29 in humans. Related research concerns collagen peptides taken by mouth. A randomised, placebo-controlled trial published in 2015 reported that daily oral collagen peptides raised skin hydration after eight weeks, and that dermal collagen density increased and fragmentation decreased within four weeks, with effects lasting through twelve weeks. Skin explants showed increased collagen and glycosaminoglycan production [3]. A 2014 randomised trial of specific bioactive collagen peptides reported reduced skin wrinkles and increased dermal matrix synthesis [4], and a 2018 randomised, double-blind trial of low-molecular-weight collagen peptide reported improvements in hydration, elasticity and wrinkling [5]. These trials involve ingested peptides, not creams. A 2024 randomised, double-blinded trial of low-molecular-weight collagen peptide supplementation likewise examined skin health [8].

Peptides taken by mouth have also been studied outside skin, with systematic reviews and trials examining collagen peptides together with training for strength, tendon remodeling, recovery from exercise and body composition.[11][12] Those studies address muscle and joint outcomes and do not test topical tripeptide-29.

Peptide serums sit within the broader market for collagen-focused skincare, in which creams, neck products and oral collagen are sold with firmness and smoothness claims. In the US these are regulated as cosmetics, so ingredient claims are not pre-approved.[1] A 2026 review of peptides in aesthetic dermatology argues that individual peptides differ in structure and function and should be considered one by one.[6]

timeline.event: Collagen mimetic peptides built from Gly-Pro-Hyp repeats are first synthesised as research tools for studying collagen. [7]
Matrixyl (palmitoyl pentapeptide), a related cosmetic signal peptide from Sederma, is launched. [2]
Randomised trials of oral collagen peptides report changes in skin hydration, elasticity and wrinkling. [4][3][5]
A review of peptides in aesthetic dermatology classifies cosmetic peptides by structure and mechanism. [6]

card.summary: A collagen-fragment peptide in firming creams that people use to make skin look firmer and smoother.

quick.overview:
Tripeptide-29 is a three-amino-acid collagen fragment used in firming skincare. People apply it to help skin look firmer and smoother.

It is found in over-the-counter serums and creams.
quick.mechanism: Suppliers describe it as a signal peptide telling skin cells to make collagen, similar in concept to other matrikine peptides [2].
quick.risks: It is a cosmetic ingredient, so claims are not pre-approved [1]. Mild irritation is possible for sensitive skin.
